title: Breakpoint chlorination, chloramines and cleaning-product cautions
audience: Pool and spa service workers and cleaners who work on or near public pools in SA. Figures and cautions apply under the state standard.
learningOutcomes: Describe the four zones of breakpoint chlorination and the point at which free chlorine appears.
Explain why chloramines cause the chlorine smell and eye irritation, and what reduces trichloramine.
Identify cleaning products that should be kept away from pools and explain why.

instruction.heading: The breakpoint process
instruction.body: Breakpoint chlorination means dosing enough free chlorine to turn chloramines and ammonia-based nitrogen compounds into harmless nitrogen gas. Chlorine is first consumed by reducing agents that are already dissolved. Adding more, the total chlorine climbs while bather-derived nitrogen compounds become monochloramines. Past a peak, further chlorine oxidises the chloramines, and total chlorine falls almost to zero. This is the breakpoint. Beyond it, extra chlorine appears as free chlorine, which is the disinfectant you want.

instruction.heading: Where chloramines come from
instruction.body: Sweat and urine bring amino acids and nitrogen-rich breakdown products into the pool. These combine with chlorine to produce monochloramines and then dichloramines. Trichloramine can form when chlorine is added before the breakpoint has been reached. Trichloramine is volatile, so it escapes into the air above the pool and causes the strong chlorine smell, and it causes severe eye irritation.

instruction.heading: Keeping pH in the band to limit trichloramine
instruction.body: Trichloramine formation increases at low pH, slows as pH rises, and is minimal between pH 7.5 and 8.0. That is one reason why the chlorine pH range is set at 7.2 and 7.6. Keep breakpoint chlorination going so trichloramine effects stay small. A strong chlorine smell is a sign of a combined chlorine problem, not of an excess of free chlorine, so check combined chlorine and pH before adding more chlorine.

instruction.heading: Cleaning products that must stay clear of the pool
instruction.body: Chlorine can react with phenolic substances to make chlorinated phenols, which irritate the eyes badly and taste unpleasant. Phenols turn up in many cleaning products, and the standard advises against using them in or near pools and spas. Keep phenolic products off the pool deck, out of pool-cleaning buckets, and away from pool equipment. Check labels on every cleaning product before you use it near a pool. Reading the label is part of the work, not an extra step.

procedure: Test free chlorine and total chlorine, and calculate the combined portion as total minus free.
Check the pH is inside the chlorine band, and correct it first if it is not.
If combined chlorine is high, follow the operator plan for breakpoint treatment, done while the water is clear of swimmers, as the shock-dose guidance sets.
Check labels on all cleaning products on site, and remove any product containing phenols from the pool zone.
Record the readings, the pH, the action taken and the product check.

workedExamples.situation: A public pool shows free chlorine 0.4 mg/L and total chlorine 2.5 mg/L. Staff complain of stinging eyes and a strong smell. A cleaner proposes a phenolic disinfectant on the pool deck.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is happening, and what should you do about the cleaner's product?
workedExamples.reasoning: Combined chlorine of about 2.1 mg/L shows chloramines have built up, and they explain the smell and the sore eyes. Breakpoint treatment is needed, as the operator plan sets. Refuse the phenolic product because it can form chlorinated phenols with chlorine and irritate the eyes badly, and escalate it to the operator.

equipmentAndPpe: Free and total chlorine test kit, in date
Cleaning product labels and safety data sheets for every product on site

commonErrors.error: Dosing more chlorine to fix the smell without checking combined chlorine or pH.
commonErrors.prevention: Measure free, total and pH first, then follow the breakpoint plan.

commonErrors.error: Using a phenolic disinfectant on the pool deck.
commonErrors.prevention: Check every product label. Keep phenolic products clear of the pool and its deck.

commonErrors.error: Adding chlorine before breakpoint is reached and expecting an immediate free reading.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the plan's sequence. Free chlorine appears only after breakpoint.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Chlorinated phenols and trichloramine both irritate the eyes badly. Keep phenolic cleaning products out of the pool zone, and check every label before use.
Chlorine and cleaning products are chemicals with safety data sheets. A licence or authorisation may apply to handling pool chemicals in your state or territory. This lesson does not grant one.
Do not enter a poorly ventilated area where chlorine smell is strong. Ventilate, leave if symptoms start, and escalate.
Figures and cautions are South Australian standard values (revised 2013). Confirm the current regulation text.

qualityStandard: Free, total and combined chlorine are recorded together at each test.
No phenolic cleaning product is used in or around the pool, and each cleaning label is checked.
Breakpoint action follows the operator plan and is carried out when no bathers are in the water.
documentationEvidence: Chlorine test record showing free, total, combined, pH and action
Cleaning product check record for the pool zone
summary: Breakpoint chlorination converts chloramines so that free chlorine can appear.
Chloramines cause the chlorine smell and eye irritation, and trichloramine rises at low pH.
Phenolic cleaning products must be kept clear of the pool and its deck.

knowledgeChecks.question: At which point in breakpoint chlorination does free chlorine begin to appear in the water?
options: At zone 1, the moment the first dose goes in
At the breakpoint, after chloramines have been oxidised
At the monochloramine peak, before any oxidation
Only when the pool is drained and refilled by hand

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is trichloramine a concern for people at the pool?
options: It raises pH above 8 and it dries out the skin
It is volatile and can irritate the eyes badly
It removes the need for filtration in the pool
It stabilises the chlorine in the spa water

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must phenolic cleaning products be kept away from pools?
options: They increase the pH and make the water smell of lemons and fruit for the bathers
They combine with chlorine to produce chlorinated phenols that irritate eyes and taste bad
They are colourless and mild, so they can be stored near the pool in the pump room
They lower total alkalinity and the pH drops fast and the water turns cloudy
